quotes: These are the complete present **eom** and preterite **wæs** series of the indicative “be.” The preterite expresses a past state. Other present forms, negative forms, moods, and nonfinite constructions will be treated separately.[9]

English pronouns label the persons. **1–3 pl.** gives the shared form for “we,” plural “you,” and “they.” No Old English pronoun forms are required for this table. Cook also gives **sind, sint** beside **sindon**.
Give the present and preterite indicative for each person and number. Use the English labels; no Old English personal pronoun is required.
current_findings.finding: The complete bounded copula is taught while OE subject pronouns are expressly excluded; COP01–06 are English-labelled conjugation prompts.
All eight independent compositions and both mini-passages use third-person noun subjects. Speaker/addressee/dual reference is unavailable for independent clauses.
Four disyllabic neuters point only to §4; ordinary light/heavy entries share hof/sǣd. Retained chapter-01.tex repeats this ambiguity at vocabulary lines 534,560,570,598.
Ten selected nominative cells sit within forty personal cells. Six first-/second-person genitives are recognition only; productive oblique reference and possession form additional systems.

recommendation.selected: Complete subject-pronoun inventory in Unit 1; retain complete four-case personal declensions and their other uses in Unit 2.
recommendation.reason: The first finite paradigm should let the learner say who is and was where across speaker, addressee and other referents. Unit 2 then contrasts familiar subjects with objects, recipients and possessors alongside independently conjugated actions.
recommendation.policy_fit: No noun declension is shortened. Unit 1 explicitly teaches the complete nominative subject inventory, not the personal declension. Unit 2 still displays every case cell.

full_declension_option.benefit: Unit 1 already teaches four noun cases, so a complete pronoun-case contrast is possible and would reduce new Unit 2 morphology.
full_declension_option.cost: Thirty extra cells beyond the subject inventory entail object/recipient ambiguity, six genitives with restricted use, and invariant possessors. Meaningful coverage would add a substantial case/reference syllabus to 44 nouns and many stem alternations, often using supplied action verbs.
full_declension_option.judgment: Coherent as a larger redesign, but the subject-first progression is better aligned to the available independent clause types, rather than merely being the smaller patch.

recommendation.rejected: Adding isolated supplied subject labels would leave independent use and completeness unresolved.

boundaries: Person means speaker/addressee/other. Pair every nominated form with the complete learned present and preterite copula.

wit/git explicitly refer to two and take ordinary plural finite forms. No dual verb ending or third-person dual is introduced. Ordinary plurals do not categorically exclude two; a requested dual target can require it.

hē/hit/hēo resume masculine/neuter/feminine singular referents; teach clear grammatical-gender examples including inanimates. English it does not mechanically require hit. hīe is common to all plural genders.
Gender/number constrain reference but do not guarantee one unique antecedent in every discourse. Keep initial contexts clear; do not turn contextual preference into a form-based certainty.
Preserve the compact 1–3 pl. verb row and display distinct subject pronouns separately or through an explicit mapped column. Shared finite spelling does not merge the pronouns.
No oblique pronoun, possessive, reflexive, adjective predicate, question, negative copula or new tense is licensed by the new subject inventory.
Use Cook-selected ðū and hīe. Valid unselected spellings remain reference alternatives, not added recall requirements.

unit2_minimal_orientation_changes.current: This unit introduces personal pronouns and the present and preterite indicative of weak verbs. Learn the finite forms in the tables, together with their stem changes. The six first- and second-person genitives and the negative verb **nabban** are for recognition. Infinitive and participle citations are available for lookup; their uses in sentences come later.
unit2_minimal_orientation_changes.change: First sentence should say the familiar subject pronouns are completed with their other cases and weak indicative verbs are introduced. Preserve remaining recognition/citation limits.

unit2_minimal_orientation_changes.current: The first person identifies the speaker; the second identifies the addressee; the third refers to someone or something else. Besides singular and plural, the first and second persons have a **dual**, explicitly referring to two. A dual subject takes the corresponding **plural verb form**; there is no separate dual verb ending. Use the dual when an exercise requests “we two” or “you two”. Ordinary plural forms are not restricted by a rule that they must always exclude two. [1]
unit2_minimal_orientation_changes.change: Mark the person/dual explanation as a short Unit 1 recap and state that complete tables repeat known nominatives alongside new obliques.

unit2_minimal_orientation_changes.current: Recognize **mīn, uncer, ūre, ðīn, incer, ēower** as genitives of the persons and numbers shown. Their corresponding possessive adjectives have endings not yet taught. Do not use this table alone to form attributive “my”, “your” or “our” phrases. Learn the remaining cells for use in the constructions below.
unit2_minimal_orientation_changes.change: Distinguish review of known nominatives from learning the new obliques in the last sentence. Keep the first/second-genitive possessive warning.
No compulsory removal. These remain useful full-system explanation and cumulative P01–P06 practice; optional review wording only.

routes.usage: Hē is masculine singular nominative. Third-person pronouns follow the grammatical gender of their referent.
Grammatical gender and antecedent determine reference; it may be represented by masculine/feminine forms for a gendered inanimate noun.
Ic is the nominative singular subject I. The governed object form me is mē in both dative and accusative.
Select case from the verb/preposition and preserve dual versus plural; dual subjects use plural verb forms.
Hit is neuter singular nominative/accusative; dative is him and genitive his. An inanimate referent of masculine or feminine grammatical gender takes the corresponding gendered pronoun instead.
Grammatical gender and antecedent determine reference; it may be represented by masculine/feminine forms for a gendered inanimate noun.
Hēo is feminine singular nominative. Third-person pronouns follow the grammatical gender of their referent.
Grammatical gender and antecedent determine reference; it may be represented by masculine/feminine forms for a gendered inanimate noun.
Hīe is plural nominative they for all genders. The plural dative is him, accusative hīe, genitive hiera.
Grammatical gender and antecedent determine reference; it may be represented by masculine/feminine forms for a gendered inanimate noun.
Wē is nominative plural we; wit is the explicitly dual we two. Both take a plural verb form.
Select case from the verb/preposition and preserve dual versus plural; dual subjects use plural verb forms.
Wit is nominative dual we two and takes a plural verb form.
Select case from the verb/preposition and preserve dual versus plural; dual subjects use plural verb forms.
Singular: nominative ðū, dative/accusative ðē; dual: nominative git, dative/accusative inc; plural: nominative gē, dative/accusative ēow. Dual subjects take plural verb forms.
Singular ðū, dual git and plural gē systems; thou/thee mark singular, ye plural. Unspecified you allows appropriate choices unless the task specifies number.
Git is nominative dual you two; inc is dative/accusative dual. A dual subject takes a plural verb form.
